The road to the observatory climbs for two hours through open desert, past salt flats that glare white at midday and go violet at dusk. At the summit sits a single telescope, a twelve-meter dish whose mirror was trucked up in sections over the course of one very long night. Astronomers come here because the desert air is dry and still, and because the nearest town large enough to throw light into the sky is four hundred kilometers away. Each night begins the same way: the dome cracks open, the telescope swings toward its first target, and someone checks the humidity for the fourth time. Work continues until the eastern rim of the desert starts to pale, when a shutter motor drives the telescope back to its parked position. Visitors are often surprised that nobody looks through the telescope at all; the light goes straight into a detector, and the images surface later on a screen in a warm room down the hill, long after the observing has ended. A second telescope, smaller and older, is kept running for teaching visits only.
